questions.q: What is the main meaning of the word "Bhakti"?
questions.a: Bhakti means "devotion" or an intense, loving surrender to God. A wrong answer suggests the student thinks it refers to a specific job or a type of building, indicating they haven't grasped the emotional nature of the term.

questions.q: Why did Bhakti saints choose to preach in the language of the common people instead of Sanskrit?
questions.a: They did this so everyone, regardless of their background, could understand the message of God directly. A wrong answer shows the student doesn't realize that Sanskrit was an exclusive language that kept most people "in the dark."

questions.q: If you were a person living in a village in the 8th century, why might you prefer a Bhakti saint over a traditional priest who only performs rituals?
questions.a: Steps: 1. Identify the priest's role (rituals). 2. Identify the saint's role (devotion/accessibility). 3. Compare the two experiences. 4. Conclude that the saint makes spirituality personal. A wrong answer reveals a failure to link "accessibility" with "personal comfort."

questions.q: How does the Bhakti movement change the role of the "priest" in society?
questions.a: It reduces the priest's authority because people no longer feel they *must* rely on an intermediary to communicate with God. A wrong answer suggests the student thinks the movement was about fighting people rather than changing ideas.

questions.q: Is the Bhakti movement more about what you do (rituals) or how you feel (love)? Defend your answer.
questions.a: It is about how you feel, because the movement explicitly emphasizes personal love and surrender over the performance of external acts. A wrong answer shows confusion between "external show" and "internal faith."

questions.q: Imagine a Bhakti saint arrives in your town today. What is one thing they might do to share their message that a textbook cannot do?
questions.a: They might sing a song in the local dialect or talk to people while they work in the fields. A poor answer is one that describes a formal lecture or a book, missing the "personal and traveling" nature of the saints.
